provenance.scheme_basis: Lagos State Government Ministry of Education Unified Scheme of Work for Primary/Basic 4, as transcribed on Syllabus.ng
provenance.database_export_finding: All 21 exported Primary 4 Home Economics third-term rows concern sewing stitches, decorative stitches or seams. The referenced scheme also includes laundry care, starch, balanced diet, deficiency/malnutrition, baking and snacks/fruit drinks; these are absent from the supplied export titles and source notes.
provenance.authoring_note: These are newly authored supplementary lessons aligned to the researched scheme topics. They do not replace or overwrite the supplied sewing lessons. The user has authorized completion and approval of this researched package after curriculum and safety review.

lessons.title: Laundry Agents, Tools and Equipment
objectives: Identify common laundry agents.
Name tools and equipment used for washing and caring for clothes.
Explain safe steps for cleaning and storing clothes.
lessons.lesson: Laundry is the work of washing, drying, ironing and storing clothes and other washable household fabrics. Laundry agents include water, soap or detergent and, where suitable, starch. Tools and equipment may include a washing bowl, bucket, clothesline, pegs, brush and iron. Clothes should be sorted according to colour and fabric type. Use the amount of detergent stated on its label, rinse clothes properly and dry them in a clean place. An adult should handle hot irons and electrical equipment.
examples: Soap and water help remove dirt.
Pegs hold clothes on a line.
An iron smooths dry clothes when used safely by an adult.
lessons.activity: Pupils sort picture cards into laundry agents, tools and equipment, then arrange the steps of washing and drying clothes in the correct order.
evaluation: What is laundry?
Name three laundry agents.
List four laundry tools or equipment.
Why should an adult handle a hot iron?

lessons.title: Starch: Preparation, Uses and Safe Application
objectives: Explain what starch is.
Identify simple materials used to prepare a starch mixture.
State uses of starch in clothing care.
lessons.lesson: Starch is a substance that can be used in clothing care to give some fabrics a firmer feel and a neat appearance. Starch may be obtained from foods such as cassava or maize. For a classroom demonstration, the teacher can prepare a simple starch mixture using a safe, suitable starch product and water. Heating and hot liquids must be handled by an adult. Starch should be used only on suitable fabrics and in the correct amount.
examples: A small amount of starch may be used when ironing some cotton clothes.
Too much starch can make fabric feel stiff.
lessons.activity: The teacher shows a prepared starch sample and a fabric sample before and after starching. Pupils describe the difference without handling hot liquid.
evaluation: What is starch used for in clothing care?
Name two possible sources of starch.
Why should pupils not handle hot starch mixtures?

lessons.title: Adequate Diet and Balanced Meals
objectives: Explain the meaning of an adequate or balanced diet.
Identify the six classes of food.
Plan a simple balanced meal using familiar local foods.
lessons.lesson: An adequate diet supplies the body with the nutrients it needs for energy, growth, repair and protection. A balanced meal includes different food groups in suitable amounts. The six classes of food are carbohydrates, proteins, fats and oils, vitamins, minerals and water. A meal can use affordable local foods such as rice, beans, vegetables, fish, eggs, fruits and clean water. A balanced diet does not have to be expensive; variety and suitable portions are important.
examples: Rice, beans, vegetables and fruit provide a variety of nutrients.
Yam with beans and leafy vegetables can form part of a balanced meal.
lessons.activity: In groups, pupils plan one day's simple menu using foods available in their community and explain which food groups are represented.
evaluation: What is a balanced diet?
Name the six classes of food.
Plan one balanced meal using local foods.
Why is variety important in meals?

lessons.title: Food Deficiency and Malnutrition
objectives: Explain deficiency and malnutrition in simple terms.
Identify examples of health problems linked to poor nutrition.
State ways of preventing malnutrition.
lessons.lesson: Malnutrition happens when a person does not get the right amount or balance of nutrients. A deficiency occurs when the body does not get enough of a particular nutrient over time. Poor nutrition can affect growth, energy and the body's ability to stay healthy. Eating a variety of foods, drinking safe water and seeking help from a health worker when unwell can help protect health. Pupils should not diagnose illness in themselves or others; concerns should be shared with a trusted adult.
examples: Not getting enough iron over time can contribute to anaemia.
Not getting enough vitamin A can affect eyesight and health.
lessons.activity: Pupils match simple food-group cards to the nutrients they provide and discuss how a varied diet helps the body.
evaluation: What is malnutrition?
What is a nutrient deficiency?
State three ways to help prevent malnutrition.
Who should a pupil tell if they are worried about their health?

lessons.title: Nutrient Deficiencies: Signs, Prevention and Healthy Choices
objectives: Recall the meaning of malnutrition and nutrient deficiency.
Give examples of health problems linked to a lack of nutrients.
Suggest healthy food choices that help prevent nutrient deficiencies.
lessons.lesson: A nutrient deficiency happens when the body does not get enough of a nutrient it needs over time. Different nutrients have different jobs, so a shortage can affect the body in different ways. For example, too little iron can contribute to anaemia, while too little vitamin A can affect eyesight and health. A varied diet with vegetables, fruits, beans, grains, eggs, fish and other suitable foods helps provide different nutrients. Food alone is not a treatment for illness; a child who feels unwell should tell a trusted adult and get advice from a health worker.
examples: Beans, leafy vegetables and some animal foods provide iron.
Orange-coloured fruits and vegetables can provide vitamin A.
Different foods together provide a wider range of nutrients.
lessons.activity: Pupils use food picture cards to plan a varied meal and identify which food groups it contains. Discuss why a health worker, not a classmate, should assess illness.
evaluation: What is a nutrient deficiency?
Name one nutrient deficiency problem and one possible effect.
Give three examples of foods that can help provide different nutrients.
Why should a child speak to a trusted adult or health worker when unwell?

lessons.title: Baking: Ingredients, Equipment and Safety
objectives: Explain baking as a cooking method.
Identify common ingredients and equipment used for baking.
State safety rules for working near an oven.
lessons.lesson: Baking is cooking food using dry heat inside an oven. A simple cake may use flour, eggs, sugar, fat and a raising agent, depending on the recipe. Equipment can include a mixing bowl, spoon, measuring cup, cake tin and oven. Ingredients should be measured carefully and handled hygienically. Only an adult should operate an oven, move hot tins or handle hot food. Pupils can take part in safe preparation tasks away from heat when supervised.
examples: Bread and cakes are baked foods.
A cake tin holds the mixture while it bakes.
lessons.activity: Pupils arrange picture cards showing the safe order of baking steps. The teacher demonstrates measuring dry ingredients without using a hot oven in the pupil activity.
evaluation: What is baking?
Name four ingredients that may be used in a simple cake.
List three items of baking equipment.
Why must an adult handle a hot oven and cake tin?

lessons.title: Snacks and Fruit Drinks: Preparation and Hygiene
objectives: Explain the meaning of snacks and fruit drinks.
Distinguish snacks from main meals.
Describe hygienic steps for preparing a simple snack or fruit drink.
lessons.lesson: A snack is a small amount of food eaten between main meals. A fruit drink is a drink made from fruit or fruit ingredients. Snacks may include boiled corn, fresh fruit or a small sandwich. Fruit should be washed with safe water and prepared with clean hands and utensils. Use clean drinking water, keep food covered and avoid fruit that is spoiled. Some people have food allergies, so ingredients should be checked and pupils should tell an adult about any known allergy.
examples: A banana can be eaten as a snack.
A fruit drink can be prepared from washed oranges and safe water.
lessons.activity: Pupils sequence picture cards for washing fruit, preparing utensils, preparing a simple snack and cleaning the work area. No tasting is required.
evaluation: What is a snack?
Give two examples of snacks.
State three differences between a snack and a main meal.
List four hygiene rules for preparing fruit drinks.
